This is real. Notice that Google doesn't provide a link to a login page. Instead, it tells you to go to your settings manually. The also email comes from @accounts.google.com, which is the verified domain for Google.

The URL microsoftonline-verify.net looks official, but it is not microsoft.com. Scammers use these 'look-alike' domains to steal your password. By also threatening to 'permanently delete' your files in 24 hours, they want you to panic so you don't notice the fake email address.

Look at the email address: hr-benefits-portal-ph.com. Scammers buy domains that look official but are not. The link also points to corporate-sso-login.com. This is a Credential Harvester. It is designed to look like a standard 'Single Sign-On' page to steal your work email and password, giving the attacker access to the entire company network.

1. Unverified Sender Number: The message comes from an unknown 11-digit mobile number (+63 999 123 4567) instead of the official, registered short-code for GCash (2882 or official GCash sender ID).
2. Shortened / Obfuscated Link: Uses a third-party link shortener (bit.ly/gcash-sec-verify) to mask the destination domain instead of pointing to the official gcash.com.
3. Informal Language & Text-Speak: Employs informal text-speak (UR account, Click here 2 verify) and repetitive phrasing, which legitimate financial institutions in the Philippines do not use in official alerts.
4. Artificial Pressure & Fearmongering: Claims the account is restricted and threatens loss of funds to trick the user into panicking and clicking the link immediately.
